nodes.title: One rule for links and pages

anchor.snippet: const can = (session: Session | null, permission: Permission | null) =>

nodes.why: The sidebar, the links inside pages and the guard all ask the same question, so they ask one function. A link the rule hides leads to a page the guard refuses, and every page the guard allows keeps its link.
nodes.alternative: Check role names where each link is drawn, such as role === 'admin'.
nodes.tradeoff: Quick to write, but it encodes today's roles: Lee, a lead, may create refunds without being an admin, so the New refund link would hide from a page Lee may open. Every new role or page also means finding every copy of the check.

nodes.title: Match whole segments
nodes.why: Comparing segment by segment gives /refunds/new its own route and its own permission, and keeps /users-export and /tickets/42/notes from borrowing the page and the permission of /users or /tickets/:id.
nodes.alternative: Match by string prefix, the first route whose path starts the address.
nodes.tradeoff: A matcher that takes the longest matching prefix opens /users-export as Users and /refunds/newest as New refund; one that takes the first prefix is worse, since /, the first route, starts every address.

nodes.title: Tell a loading session from a signed-out one
nodes.why: Before fetchSession answers, the app does not know who is there. Treating that as signed out rewrites the address to /sign-in and shows the sign-in page to a user who is already signed in, and refuses or allows pages on a guess; a third state shows a short loading view and keeps the address.
nodes.alternative: Render the page at once and redirect if the session turns out not to allow it.
nodes.tradeoff: The page appears sooner for users who may open it, but anyone else sees it, and its data loads, before the redirect.

nodes.title: Decide in render, redirect after the commit
nodes.why: The guard returns the redirect instead of the page, so the page never mounts and never loads its data. A guard that renders its children and redirects from its own effect is too late: React runs the children's effects before the parent's, so the page has loaded by then. The redirect itself runs in a layout effect, after the commit and before the browser paints, so no empty frame shows between the refused address and the Dashboard.
nodes.alternative: Render the children and redirect in a useEffect in the guard.
nodes.tradeoff: It reads naturally, but every refused page mounts for one commit: it loads its data, and anything it shows flashes on screen.

nodes.title: Replace the entry instead of pushing
nodes.why: A redirect replaces the entry that asked for the refused page, so Back goes to the page before it. Pushing keeps the refused path in the history: Back returns to it, the guard redirects again, and the user cannot leave by Back.
nodes.tradeoff: Push keeps a record of the refused visit, but that record is a trap: each Back lands on the redirect again.

nodes.title: Let the sign-in entry carry the return path
nodes.why: The /sign-in entry carries the path that sent the user there. A signed-in user on that entry goes to it, and a /sign-in typed later remembers nothing, so it leads to the Dashboard instead of a page asked for long ago.
nodes.alternative: Put the return path in the address, as /sign-in?next=/audit-log.
nodes.tradeoff: A query string survives a reload and can be shared, but the app must then check that it is a path on this site, or a crafted link sends users elsewhere after they sign in. This exercise keeps the address at /sign-in, and the checks expect it to read exactly that.

nodes.title: End the notice at the next navigation
nodes.why: The notice explains one redirect. It lives in App state: the refusing redirect sets it right after its replace, and a history listener clears it at every navigation, Back included, so it does not come back when Back returns to that Dashboard. The listener runs at the navigation itself; an effect in App that compared keys would run after the child's redirect but still see the key App rendered with, and clear the notice that was just set.
nodes.alternative: Store the refused page's title in the Dashboard entry's state.
nodes.tradeoff: It needs no extra state, but the notice then lives as long as the entry, and Back to that entry shows a refusal the user did not just meet.

nodes.title: Follow the session through onSessionChange

anchor.snippet: const stop = onSessionChange((session) => setState({ status: 'ready', session }));

nodes.why: Sign-in and sign-out start on this page, but a role change need not: here a saved role reaches the session a moment after the save, and in a real app another admin or an expiring token changes it too. Listening to the server keeps one path for all of them, and the cleanup stops the listener when App unmounts.
nodes.alternative: Set the session from the results of signIn and signOut.
nodes.tradeoff: It works for the changes this page starts and misses every other one, so a demoted user keeps their old sidebar and stays on a page they may no longer open.

nodes.title: Mark the section, not every prefix
nodes.why: A child page names its sidebar link in section, so /tickets/42 marks Tickets and nothing else. Comparing prefixes would mark Dashboard on every page, since every path starts with /.
nodes.alternative: Mark each link whose path starts the address.
nodes.tradeoff: It needs no extra field, but / starts every address, so Dashboard is always marked, and two links can claim one page.

nodes.title: Give each path its own page instance
nodes.why: Going from /users/1/edit to /users/2/edit renders the same component. Keying it by path mounts a fresh one, so the role picked for one user does not carry over to the next, and the page loads its data again.
nodes.alternative: Keep one instance and reset its state in an effect when params change.
nodes.tradeoff: It avoids a remount, but each page must remember to reset every piece of its state, and it first renders once with the old values.
